title: Your own notebook
hookLine: Marcus wrote to himself, and so can you

lines: NOTES APP, VOICE MEMO, A RECEIPT.
cards: Notes app, a voice memo, the back of a receipt. Plenty of people write to themselves: grocery lists, reminders, half a thought at 2am. None of it is meant for anyone else, and much of it gets deleted.

Marcus Aurelius did something similar, in Greek, and by the book's own headings, some of it in army camps on the frontier. He didn't write for us. He wrote to himself, the way you'd leave a note on the fridge.

teach.b: First, the title. In the old manuscripts the book is called Ta eis heauton: the things to himself. Scholars doubt Marcus gave it that name, but it fits.
Meditations is a later English title. Second, the place.

teach.h: WRITTEN ON CAMPAIGN BY A RIVER.
teach.b: Two of the books carry little headings: one written among the Quadi, by the river Granua; another at Carnuntum, an army base on the Danube.
So at least some of it was written on campaign, by an emperor at war on the frontier, not in a library.
Third, the voice. Read any page and it's you: you'll meet difficult people today; you're getting angry again; remember. He isn't explaining Stoicism to a reader.
He's coaching the one person who most needs it, and he's honest with him. He repeats himself, scolds himself, changes his mind. That's what a notebook is for.
Fourth, why it works. Writing a rule down is different from knowing it.
The pen slows you down and makes the vague thing exact. And your own words, reread later in your own handwriting, land differently from anyone else's.
Marcus wasn't writing a classic. He was practicing, the way a musician practices scales, and the practice happened to be on paper. No Greek, no empire, no audience required.
Three honest lines to yourself are already a notebook.

how: Many people who read Marcus keep a private notebook of their own, writing short reminders to themselves in the second person and rereading them.

games.q: you want to keep a notebook like Marcus's. what do you write first?
o: a polished essay for others to read.
three honest lines to yourself, using "you."
games.why: Marcus coached himself in plain second-person reminders. no audience, no polish, just practice on paper.

practice: If you have paper or the notes on your phone, write three lines to yourself the way Marcus did, using you: one about something you keep forgetting, one about a person you'll see today, one about what matters most this week.
Don't make them pretty; make them true. Then read them back once, slowly, as if someone who loves you wrote them.

wordCard.voice: Carnuntum. One of the army camps on the Danube frontier where Marcus is thought to have written parts of his notebook to himself. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: to myself. The notebook was never meant for anyone else. Good to see you today.
